title: Vibe Coding 03 — Secure Application Engineering
description: Build usable interfaces, trustworthy HTTP APIs, well-modeled databases, security controls, and falsifiable tests. Each activity connects a concrete implementation decision to verification. Part 3 of 5.

paths.title: Frontend, UI & UX Design
paths.description: Build AI-generated interfaces that are coherent, responsive, accessible, state-complete, and grounded in a design system.

paths.title: Backend & API Engineering
paths.description: Generate server-side code with explicit contracts, validation, authorization, idempotency, reliability, and operational behavior.

paths.title: Databases, Data Modeling & Migrations
paths.description: Design persistent data deliberately so AI-generated features preserve integrity, privacy, performance, and recoverability.

paths.title: Security, Privacy & Threat Modeling
paths.description: Apply secure design and current web-application risk controls to AI-generated software instead of treating security as a final scan.

paths.title: Testing Strategy & Verification
paths.description: Use layered automated and manual evidence to prove AI-generated behavior rather than trusting compilation or model confidence.

cards.title: Design before styling
cards.prompt: Why should an interface's task hierarchy be defined before visual styling begins?
cards.content: A polished screen can still have a broken information hierarchy. Define user goals, content hierarchy, primary actions, and states before visual decoration.

cards.title: Use a design system
cards.prompt: Which design tokens and components should a generated screen reuse?
cards.content: Ad hoc component generation creates inconsistency. Reuse tokens, typography, spacing, colors, controls, and interaction patterns.

cards.title: Define responsive behavior
cards.prompt: What must a responsive specification say about navigation and content at narrow widths?
cards.content: Desktop screenshots do not specify mobile behavior. Describe how layout, navigation, content density, and controls adapt across available space.

cards.title: Design all interaction states
cards.prompt: What sequence ensures a generated control has all essential interaction states?
cards.content: Controls need more than default appearance. Specify hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, success, error, and empty states.
steps: Define its role, action, and accessible name.
Design default, hover (where applicable), keyboard focus, and active states.
Define disabled or unavailable behavior without hiding necessary information.
Add loading, success, error, and retry states for asynchronous actions.
Test the state transitions with keyboard and assistive technology.

cards.title: Preserve semantic HTML
cards.prompt: A generated screen uses clickable div elements for saving and text spans for navigation. What is the more robust semantic structure?

options: Add role=button to each div and leave keyboard behavior to the browser.
Use generic divs with both click and keydown handlers, but omit link semantics and href.
Use a button for commands and an anchor with href for navigation.
Turn both controls into anchors with no href to preserve their common styling.
question.explanation: Native semantics improve accessibility and resilience. Use buttons for actions, links for navigation, labels for form controls, and landmarks for page structure. Native controls bring expected semantics, keyboard behavior, and focus handling.

cards.title: Make keyboard use complete
cards.prompt: How can keyboard users complete every critical action without a pointer?
cards.content: Clickable visuals are not enough. Ensure all actions are reachable, operable, and visibly focused without a pointer.

cards.title: Manage focus intentionally
cards.prompt: Where should focus move when a dialog opens and after it closes?
cards.content: Dialogs, route changes, errors, and dynamic content can disorient keyboard and screen-reader users. Move and restore focus according to the interaction context.

cards.title: Use clear form validation
cards.prompt: What makes inline form validation understandable and recoverable?
cards.content: Users need to know what failed and how to fix it. Connect field errors to inputs, preserve entered data, and validate authoritatively on the server.

cards.title: Avoid layout shift
cards.prompt: Why must asynchronous images and content reserve layout space?
cards.content: Late-loading content can move controls under the user. Reserve space for media and async content and use stable skeletons when useful.

cards.title: Design meaningful loading
cards.prompt: How can a loading indicator communicate progress without misleading the user?
cards.content: Indefinite spinners provide little information. Use immediate feedback, progress where knowable, and optimistic UI only when rollback is safe.

cards.title: Design empty states as onboarding
cards.prompt: What should an empty state explain to someone using the feature for the first time?
cards.content: An empty product surface should help users begin. Explain why the space is empty and present the next useful action.

cards.title: Respect reduced motion
cards.prompt: The CSS snippet uses prefers-reduced-motion. Which preference does it honor, and what interaction must remain available?
cards.content: Motion should not block or distress users. Honor user preferences and avoid unnecessary parallax, flashing, or large movement.

cards.title: Optimize text readability
cards.prompt: Which typography decisions improve readability on smaller devices?
cards.content: Generated interfaces often overuse tiny muted text. Use sufficient contrast, readable line length, clear hierarchy, and scalable text.

cards.title: Treat errors as product states
cards.prompt: What should a product-level error state tell the user after an API failure?
cards.content: Technical messages rarely help users. Translate failures into actionable language without hiding support-relevant context.

cards.title: Use optimistic UI carefully
cards.prompt: When can an optimistic UI create a misleading state, and what is its recovery plan?
cards.content: Fast-feeling interfaces can lie when operations fail. Apply optimistic updates only when conflicts and rollback are well-defined.

cards.title: Preserve URL state where useful
cards.prompt: Which UI state belongs in the URL so it survives navigation and sharing?
cards.content: Shareable and restorable application state improves usability. Represent navigable selections, filters, or resources in URLs when appropriate.

cards.title: Test with real content extremes
cards.prompt: Which real-world content extremes should be included in responsive visual testing?
cards.content: Placeholder text hides overflow and density problems. Use long names, empty values, large numbers, translated strings, and many items during UI validation.

cards.title: Avoid generic AI aesthetics
cards.prompt: How can a product avoid polished-looking but inconsistent generated UI patterns?
cards.content: Repeated gradients, oversized hero text, and decorative clutter can weaken product identity. Ground generated designs in the actual brand, audience, content, and product purpose.

cards.title: Validate visually and functionally
cards.prompt: Before accepting a generated page, which visual and functional checks should pass?
cards.content: A DOM that compiles can still render incorrectly. Use browser verification across key viewport sizes, interactions, and error states.
items: Mobile, tablet, and desktop layouts preserve hierarchy and readable text.
Keyboard traversal, focus indicators, accessible names, and form errors work.
Slow-network, empty, failure, and long-content states render correctly.
No destructive action can be triggered accidentally.
A real-browser check finds no console error or unexpected layout shift.

cards.title: Optimize the full journey
cards.prompt: How do you evaluate the full journey rather than one attractive screenshot?
cards.content: Local component quality does not guarantee a coherent product. Review navigation, task completion, recovery, and consistency across the entire user flow.

cards.title: Validate at trust boundaries
cards.prompt: What should an API do with an untrusted request before changing data?
cards.content: External input is untrusted regardless of client validation. Parse and validate request bodies, parameters, headers, files, and external service data on the server.
steps: Authenticate the caller when the route requires identity.
Parse and validate syntax, type, size, and permitted field values.
Authorize the action against the actual target resource and tenant.
Apply business invariants and an atomic write or retry-safe contract.
Return a documented outcome without leaking internal details.

cards.title: Separate authentication and authorization
cards.prompt: A signed-in user attempts to delete a project owned by another account. Which server-side check is still required?

options: Only verify that a session cookie exists.
Check authorization against the requested project and actor before deletion.
Trust the frontend because it hid the delete button.
Treat authentication as proof of ownership.
question.explanation: Knowing who a caller is does not imply what they may do. Authenticate identity, then enforce resource- and action-specific authorization. Authentication establishes an identity; authorization decides whether that identity can perform this action on this resource.

cards.title: Use resource ownership checks
cards.prompt: How should a service confirm ownership before returning or mutating a record?
cards.content: Object-level authorization failures expose other users' data. Verify tenant, owner, membership, or policy for every sensitive resource access.

cards.title: Return meaningful HTTP semantics
cards.prompt: Which HTTP statuses distinguish malformed, forbidden, missing, and successful requests?
cards.content: Clients need predictable status behavior. Use methods and status codes consistently and include machine-readable error structures.

cards.title: Design idempotency for retries
cards.prompt: In the illustrative payment route, what property must createOnce enforce for the Idempotency-Key to make client retries safe?
cards.content: Clients and infrastructure may retry requests. Protect create, payment, and side-effecting operations with idempotency mechanisms when repetition is unsafe.

cards.title: Bound request work
cards.prompt: When should an API reject, paginate, defer, or time out expensive work?
cards.content: Long or unbounded requests consume capacity and fail unpredictably. Use limits, timeouts, pagination, and background jobs for expensive work.

cards.title: Protect against N+1 access
cards.prompt: How can a query that looks simple accidentally issue one database call per returned row?
cards.content: Generated data-fetching code can perform one query per item. Batch, join, prefetch, or otherwise bound database calls on list endpoints.

cards.title: Use transactions for invariants
cards.prompt: Which multi-step business updates must commit or roll back together?
cards.content: Related writes can partially succeed without atomicity. Wrap operations that must commit together in a database transaction.

cards.title: Handle partial external failure
cards.prompt: How should an API recover when its database succeeds but an external service times out?
cards.content: Third-party APIs can timeout or return inconsistent errors. Define retry classes, timeouts, circuit behavior, and compensation for side effects.

cards.title: Design rate limits
cards.prompt: What identity and resource should a rate limit key protect?
cards.content: Public endpoints can be abused even when functionally correct. Limit by appropriate identity and operation while returning useful retry information.

cards.title: Use structured errors
cards.prompt: What error contract helps clients recover without exposing implementation details?
cards.content: String-only errors are hard to automate and localize. Return stable error codes with safe messages and correlation identifiers.

cards.title: Avoid leaking internals
cards.prompt: Why should a public API never expose stack traces or internal credentials?
cards.content: Stack traces and database errors reveal implementation details. Log detailed diagnostics server-side and return bounded public errors.

cards.title: Make pagination deterministic
cards.prompt: How should pagination ensure stable ordering when rows are inserted concurrently?
cards.content: Unstable ordering can duplicate or skip results. Use explicit stable order and cursor-based pagination where data changes frequently.

cards.title: Version contracts deliberately
cards.prompt: When does a backwards-incompatible API change require explicit versioning?
cards.content: Clients may outlive a backend deployment. Prefer additive changes and introduce explicit versions when compatibility cannot be preserved.

cards.title: Protect webhook endpoints
cards.prompt: How should an incoming webhook's authenticity and replay behavior be validated?
cards.content: Webhook requests come from outside the trust boundary. Verify signatures, timestamps, replay protection, and event idempotency.

cards.title: Use background jobs safely
cards.prompt: Which tasks belong in a durable background queue instead of an HTTP request?
cards.content: Queues add retry and duplication semantics. Make jobs idempotent, observable, bounded, and dead-lettered when repeated failure requires inspection.

cards.title: Implement graceful shutdown
cards.prompt: What must a server do with in-flight work when it receives a shutdown signal?
cards.content: Deployments should not abandon accepted work. Stop new traffic, drain in-flight requests or jobs, and close resources within a timeout.

cards.title: Expose liveness and readiness separately
cards.prompt: What is the distinction between a live process and a ready-to-serve instance?
cards.content: A running process may not be able to serve traffic. Use readiness for required dependencies and liveness for process recovery decisions.

cards.title: Document API examples
cards.prompt: What examples should API documentation include besides a happy-path request?
cards.content: Contracts are easier to use when examples match the schema. Keep representative requests, responses, errors, and authentication examples current.

cards.title: Test contracts at boundaries
cards.prompt: Which contract-boundary tests should pass before releasing an AI-generated endpoint?
cards.content: Backend correctness depends on more than unit logic. Add integration tests for validation, permissions, persistence, external adapters, and failure responses.
items: Malformed inputs receive consistent validation errors.
An authenticated but unauthorized caller cannot access another resource.
Missing and duplicate requests have documented semantics.
Transactional failure does not leave half-written authoritative state.
Success and error response shapes remain compatible with supported clients.

cards.title: Model entities from domain meaning
cards.prompt: How should a domain entity be identified before deciding its table layout?
cards.content: Tables should represent stable concepts, not whatever shape the first UI used. Identify entities, ownership, relationships, lifecycle, and invariants before writing schema.

cards.title: Use database constraints
cards.prompt: Which invalid states should the database reject even if a frontend has already validated input?
cards.content: Application checks alone are vulnerable to races and alternate code paths. Enforce uniqueness, foreign keys, nullability, and valid ranges at the database where appropriate.

cards.title: Choose keys deliberately
cards.prompt: Why are stable identifiers preferable to mutable business attributes as primary keys?
cards.content: Identifier design affects references, exposure, and distribution. Use stable primary keys and avoid leaking sensitive sequencing when public identifiers matter.

cards.title: Represent ownership explicitly
cards.prompt: How should a membership schema represent user-to-project roles and ownership?
cards.content: Multi-user data requires a clear security model. Store tenant or owner relationships needed for authorization and query scoping.

cards.title: Normalize before denormalizing
cards.prompt: How do normalization and intentional denormalization affect update anomalies?
cards.content: Duplicated fields create synchronization obligations. Start with a clear source of truth and denormalize only for measured performance or product needs.

cards.title: Index query patterns
cards.prompt: What query workload evidence justifies creating a new index?
cards.content: Indexes should follow actual filters, joins, and ordering. Use query plans and workload evidence rather than indexing every column.

cards.title: Understand transaction isolation
cards.prompt: Two transactions may read and update the same account concurrently. How should isolation be chosen?

options: Use READ COMMITTED for every workload because it is a common default.
Choose the isolation level entirely from the expected latency budget.
Assume transaction retries alone eliminate all write anomalies.
Choose a level that prevents the anomalies relevant to the business invariant, then test it.
question.explanation: Concurrent operations can observe or overwrite unexpected states. Choose locking or isolation based on the invariants the transaction must protect. Isolation is a deliberate correctness and concurrency trade-off, not a universal one-size-fits-all setting.

cards.title: Use safe schema migrations
cards.prompt: Read the staged SQL migration. Why do compatible application deployment and backfill occur before old-field removal?
cards.content: Breaking schema changes can outpace deployed application versions. Prefer expand-migrate-contract and keep old and new code compatible during rollout.

code.snippet:
ALTER TABLE account ADD COLUMN display_name_v2 text;
-- deploy compatible code
-- backfill in bounded batches
-- switch reads
-- remove legacy field in a later release

cards.title: Backfill in bounded batches
cards.prompt: How do you backfill a new column without a long, fragile write transaction?
cards.content: Large data rewrites can lock tables or exhaust resources. Batch, throttle, checkpoint, and observe long-running backfills.
steps: Deploy the additive column and compatible reads/writes first.
Select a bounded batch by stable cursor or key.
Write idempotently and record durable batch progress.
Throttle and monitor latency, locks, replication, and data quality.
Resume on interruption; verify completion before switching authoritative reads.

cards.title: Make migrations deterministic
cards.prompt: What makes a migration repeatable and safe to re-execute after interruption?
cards.content: Environment-dependent migrations are difficult to reproduce. Avoid time-sensitive or network-dependent migration logic and keep migration history immutable after release.

cards.title: Separate schema and seed data
cards.prompt: How should sample seed data be separated from schema and production data?
cards.content: Reference data and test fixtures have different lifecycle requirements. Version production reference data intentionally and keep development seeds safe to rerun.

cards.title: Protect sensitive fields
cards.prompt: Which sensitive database fields need strict access, retention, and logging controls?
cards.content: Not every persisted value should be equally accessible. Classify personal, credential, financial, and confidential data and minimize collection.

cards.title: Encrypt where threat models require it
cards.prompt: When is encryption relevant, and what additional key-management choices are necessary?
cards.content: Encryption is useful only with proper key management and access boundaries. Use established platform encryption and rotate keys according to policy.

cards.title: Define retention and deletion
cards.prompt: Which conditions determine when records and backups should be deleted?
cards.content: Data should not live forever by accident. Specify retention periods, account deletion semantics, backups, and legal holds.

cards.title: Use soft delete carefully
cards.prompt: When does soft deletion complicate uniqueness, queries, and legal retention?
cards.content: Soft-deleted rows can leak into queries and remain personally identifiable. Use it only when recovery or audit needs justify the ongoing complexity.

cards.title: Validate backup restoration
cards.prompt: What evidence makes a database backup a credible recovery mechanism?
cards.content: A backup is not proven until it can restore service. Test restore procedures and measure recovery time and recovery point objectives.
items: The backup includes needed schema, application metadata, and credentials or key recovery procedures.
An isolated restore has completed successfully.
Integrity checks and representative queries work on restored data.
Recovery time and acceptable data-loss objectives are measured.
The restore procedure is documented and repeated after material changes.

cards.title: Monitor query performance
cards.prompt: Which query metrics show whether the live workload is deteriorating?
cards.content: Generated queries may be correct but operationally expensive. Track slow queries, row counts, plans, lock contention, and connection saturation.

cards.title: Control connection pools
cards.prompt: How do connection-pool limits prevent an application from overwhelming its database?
cards.content: Too many connections can overwhelm a database. Size pools per instance and deployment topology, and release connections promptly.

cards.title: Avoid production data in local prompts
cards.prompt: Why must local AI prompts not contain raw production records unnecessarily?
cards.content: Real user data can create privacy and security exposure. Use synthetic or properly anonymized datasets for debugging and AI context.

cards.title: Test migrations both directions operationally
cards.prompt: What operational tests should accompany a forward migration and a rollback plan?
cards.content: Schema evolution must work across realistic deploy sequences. Validate upgrade, mixed-version operation, data backfill, and rollback or forward-fix strategy.

cards.title: Threat model important features
cards.prompt: How do you threat-model a new AI-assisted upload feature before implementation?
cards.content: Security starts by understanding assets, actors, trust boundaries, and abuse paths. Identify what can be stolen, modified, impersonated, exhausted, or bypassed before implementation.
steps: Identify uploaded data, downstream processing, and exposed assets.
Map trust boundaries for browser, API, storage, scanners, and workers.
List plausible actors and abuse cases including malicious file contents and broken access control.
Select size/type checks, authorization, isolation, and retention controls.
Convert threat scenarios into negative and integration tests.

cards.title: Enforce least privilege
cards.prompt: How can least privilege limit the damage from a compromised account or agent?
cards.content: Excess permission increases blast radius. Give users, services, tokens, and database roles only the access needed for their task.

cards.title: Prevent broken access control
cards.prompt: In this illustrative project-lookup guard, why does the ownerId comparison matter even for an authenticated caller?
cards.content: Authorization mistakes remain a leading web risk. Check permissions server-side for every sensitive object and action, including indirect identifiers.

cards.title: Secure default configuration
cards.prompt: Which secure defaults should be applied before a feature becomes externally reachable?
cards.content: Development-friendly defaults can be unsafe in production. Disable debug exposure, unnecessary services, permissive CORS, and default credentials.

cards.title: Protect the software supply chain
cards.prompt: What package and build-chain risks must be evaluated for AI-suggested dependencies?
cards.content: Dependencies and build inputs can introduce compromised code. Pin important dependencies, review changes, scan advisories, and secure build provenance.

cards.title: Use approved cryptography
cards.prompt: Why is custom cryptography generally an unacceptable shortcut in generated code?
cards.content: Custom cryptographic code is difficult to design and review correctly. Use established libraries, algorithms, key management, and platform primitives.

cards.title: Prevent injection
cards.prompt: An AI-generated endpoint concatenates a user-provided search string into SQL. What remediation addresses the injection boundary?

options: Escape quote characters manually and keep SQL string concatenation.
Limit string length without separating input values from query syntax.
Use parameterized queries or a safe query builder with input validation.
Require a signed-in user but keep interpolating the query directly.
question.explanation: Untrusted input must not become executable syntax. Use parameterized queries, safe APIs, contextual output encoding, and strict command construction. Validation supports domain rules; parameter binding keeps supplied values from becoming query syntax.

cards.title: Design security into workflows
cards.prompt: Where should security review be embedded in the change and release workflow?
cards.content: Security controls bolted on later leave structural gaps. Include authorization, sensitive data, abuse resistance, and failure behavior in acceptance criteria.

cards.title: Harden authentication
cards.prompt: How can login, recovery, and session establishment resist common account attacks?
cards.content: Account takeover risk extends beyond password validation. Use proven identity providers or libraries, secure sessions, MFA where appropriate, and safe recovery.

cards.title: Protect secrets
cards.prompt: How should application, CI, and cloud credentials be provisioned and rotated?
cards.content: Keys and credentials should never be committed or exposed to clients. Use secret managers or protected environment injection, rotate leaks, and enable scanning or push protection.

cards.title: Use secure session cookies
cards.prompt: What protections should an authenticated session cookie include?
cards.content: Browser sessions need transport and script protections. Set Secure, HttpOnly, appropriate SameSite, bounded lifetime, and server-side invalidation behavior.

cards.title: Protect against CSRF where relevant
cards.prompt: When must state-changing browser requests defend against cross-site request forgery?
cards.content: Cookie-authenticated state changes can be triggered cross-site. Use SameSite protections and CSRF tokens or equivalent defenses for susceptible flows.

cards.title: Defend against XSS
cards.prompt: How can unsafe output rendering turn stored user text into executable script?
cards.content: Rendering untrusted content into HTML or script contexts can execute attacker code. Prefer framework escaping, sanitize rich content, and use a restrictive Content Security Policy.

cards.title: Validate uploaded files
cards.prompt: What should file-upload validation check beyond the declared filename?
cards.content: File extensions are not trustworthy security boundaries. Check size, content type, storage location, processing, access control, and malware risk.

cards.title: Rate-limit abuse-sensitive actions
cards.prompt: Which endpoints particularly require user- and resource-sensitive rate limiting?
cards.content: Login, reset, invite, search, and expensive endpoints can be automated maliciously. Rate limit by appropriate identities and add abuse monitoring for high-value workflows.

cards.title: Log security events safely
cards.prompt: What can a security audit log record without leaking credentials or personal data?
cards.content: Detection requires useful signals without leaking secrets. Log authentication, authorization, configuration, and sensitive actions with correlation and redaction.

cards.title: Fail closed for sensitive decisions
cards.prompt: How should a sensitive authorization decision behave when its dependency fails?
cards.content: Exceptional conditions should not accidentally grant access or skip controls. Choose safe fallback behavior for permission, verification, payment, and integrity failures.

cards.title: Minimize personal data
cards.prompt: Which data-minimization questions should be answered before storing a new user field?
cards.content: The safest sensitive data is data you never collect. Collect only what the product needs and define retention, deletion, and access rules.
items: The collection purpose is explicit and justified.
Only needed fields are requested, with appropriate access controls.
Retention, deletion, backup, and export behavior are defined.
Logs, prompts, and analytics do not duplicate unnecessary sensitive data.
Data subjects and operators can follow an appropriate correction/deletion process.

cards.title: Review AI-generated dependencies
cards.prompt: What permissions and vulnerabilities must be checked before accepting an AI-proposed package?
cards.content: Models may suggest outdated, typo-squatted, or nonexistent packages. Verify package identity, maintenance, license, provenance, and security before installation.

cards.title: Re-review security after changes
cards.prompt: Why must threat assumptions be revisited after changes to auth, data flow, or tooling?
cards.content: Security assumptions can break when code evolves. Run static analysis, dependency checks, focused tests, and human review on high-risk diffs.

cards.title: Test behavior, not implementation trivia
cards.prompt: Which public behavior should a test protect while allowing internal refactoring?
cards.content: Tests should protect meaningful outcomes while allowing internal refactoring. Assert public behavior, state transitions, contracts, and important side effects.

cards.title: Build a testing pyramid pragmatically
cards.prompt: How do focused unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end journeys complement one another?
cards.content: Fast tests support iteration; broader tests protect integration. Use many focused unit tests, boundary integration tests, and a smaller set of critical end-to-end journeys.

cards.title: Write tests from acceptance criteria
cards.prompt: How should acceptance criteria be translated into an executable test suite?
cards.content: Requirements are strongest when they become executable evidence. Map each important acceptance scenario to one or more automated or explicit manual checks.
steps: Extract each user-observable promise and forbidden behavior.
Choose the narrowest test layer capable of proving it.
Prepare deterministic normal, boundary, and failure fixtures.
Assert outcomes and authoritative side effects rather than implementation trivia.
Track the executed evidence against each acceptance scenario.

cards.title: Test negative cases
cards.prompt: Which test case most directly checks a previously ignored failure path?

options: Test that an authorized user receives a normal success response.
Test that a mocked endpoint can display a generic error message.
Compare the happy-path UI snapshot before and after the change.
An unauthorized caller gets denied without changing the database.
question.explanation: Happy-path tests miss many production defects. Cover invalid input, permissions, missing resources, timeouts, conflicts, and dependency failures. A negative test must verify the prohibited effect did not occur, not just an error message.

cards.title: Test boundaries
cards.prompt: What minimum, maximum, empty, and just-outside values should a boundary test include?
cards.content: Off-by-one and threshold defects are common in generated code. Exercise empty, minimum, maximum, just-inside, and just-outside values.

cards.title: Test authorization separately
cards.prompt: The authorization test expects 403 and unchanged persistence. What different security properties do these two assertions verify?
cards.content: A feature can work functionally while exposing data. Verify each role against allowed and forbidden resources and actions.

cards.title: Test persistence behavior
cards.prompt: Why do critical persistence tests need a representative database instead of only mocks?
cards.content: Mocks can hide schema, transaction, and query problems. Use integration tests against a representative database for critical data flows.

cards.title: Test external adapters
cards.prompt: What behavior should an external API adapter simulate under timeout and partial failure?
cards.content: Third-party contracts fail in unusual ways. Simulate success, retryable errors, permanent errors, slow responses, malformed payloads, and duplicate events.

cards.title: Use deterministic fixtures
cards.prompt: How do fixed clocks, seeds, and fixtures make a test repeatable?
cards.content: Flaky randomness erodes confidence. Control clocks, seeds, identifiers, external calls, and test data.

cards.title: Avoid over-mocking
cards.prompt: What important behavior can be accidentally excluded by excessive mocking?
cards.content: Mocks that duplicate implementation assumptions can make broken systems appear green. Mock true external boundaries and exercise real internal collaboration where practical.

cards.title: Use property-based tests where useful
cards.prompt: When can generated inputs or property-based tests discover unanticipated edge cases?
cards.content: Some rules span many possible inputs. Generate diverse inputs for parsers, serializers, invariants, and mathematical properties.

cards.title: Use snapshot tests selectively
cards.prompt: Why are snapshots a poor replacement for intentional behavioral assertions?
cards.content: Large snapshots can approve accidental changes blindly. Keep snapshots focused and review diffs rather than updating them reflexively.

cards.title: Test migrations
cards.prompt: Which migrations should be exercised against realistic prior schema states?
cards.content: Schema code should be verified like application code. Apply migrations from realistic prior states and test mixed-version compatibility where relevant.

cards.title: Test concurrency
cards.prompt: How should an idempotency test prove that a retry creates only one committed effect?
cards.content: Single-threaded tests cannot reveal all race conditions. Exercise duplicate submissions, conflicting edits, locking, and idempotency.

cards.title: Test performance budgets
cards.prompt: Which latency or throughput thresholds should be checked under realistic conditions?
cards.content: Functionally correct code can still fail at scale. Add benchmarks or load checks for hot paths with meaningful thresholds.

cards.title: Test accessibility
cards.prompt: How should keyboard and assistive-technology behavior enter the test plan?
cards.content: Automated checks catch only part of accessibility. Combine automated scanning with keyboard, focus, semantics, and screen-reader checks.

cards.title: Use visual regression where valuable
cards.prompt: When does visual regression testing add value beyond DOM assertions?
cards.content: UI refactors can change appearance without DOM failures. Capture stable critical components or flows and review meaningful visual differences.

cards.title: Run focused checks during iteration
cards.prompt: Which focused tests should run immediately after a narrow change?
cards.content: Fast feedback keeps the agent aligned. Run the smallest relevant test set after each coherent change before full-suite validation.

cards.title: Run the full gate before merge
cards.prompt: Which checks form the final pre-merge verification gate?
cards.content: Local focused success does not prove repository-wide compatibility. Execute required lint, types, tests, build, security, and integration checks on the final head.
items: Unit and integration checks pass on the exact proposed head.
Critical end-to-end, accessibility, and security paths run as applicable.
Schema migrations and persistence invariants are verified.
The diff contains no weakened tests or unjustified skipped checks.
Build and deployment-sensitive checks are reported with actual outcomes.

cards.title: Treat failing tests as evidence
cards.prompt: What should an engineer infer from a failed test before modifying an assertion?
cards.content: A failing test is information about either code or an outdated requirement. Investigate the reason before changing production code or weakening the assertion.
